doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Burning out on show gigs with Raquel Welch and Tony Orlando
summary: He chose career over art; Welch and Orlando shows meant repetitive music, and he left Orlando in 1985 when work thinned.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Well I’ve heard other people — Herb Ellis said the same thing. He said you should be singing — be able to sing what you want to play I guess. But he apparently did the same thing, he would sing along. So did you eventually get burned out with the road and being away?

You know I did and I think a lot of it had to do with I kind of made a choice to become a career musician rather than a dedicated artist. And this is something that happens to a lot of people. If you’re lucky enough to play the kind of music professionally that you want to play to the exclusion of everything else, then you’re dedicated to your craft, you’re dedicated to your art, and you go where that takes you. But you’re happy doing what you’re doing and you’re not worried about well let’s see I have to support a family, I’ve got to do this, I’ve got to do that. These other elements kind of force you, or at least it forced me to do things that you don’t necessarily want to do, you say well this is temporary. So the Lou Rawls gig was for the most part musically rewarding. I enjoyed what I was doing. The next two professional gigs I had were show gigs. I had Raquel Welch’s gig, which was a show. It was world-class musicians, but we were playing a show. And then Tony Orlando, a wonderful person to me, very good to me, but it’s a show, playing the kind of music that I really didn’t want to play, but again I was playing with great musicians, we were doing first-class gigs, and we were making decent bucks. So you say well, you know, if I can keep doing this, at some point maybe I’ll find another professional gig that I really want to play, but if that doesn’t happen, which in my case it really didn’t, you’re playing “Tie a Yellow Ribbon” two nights — you know, seven © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

nights a week, two shows a night. You know you can burn out on that stuff because you’re not playing what you want to play anyway, and yet you’re doing it all over the country, all over the world, and you’re not home, and all the negatives take on more importance. So yeah, burn out happens. And you get to the point where you say I’d rather do something else, not necessarily rather do something other than music, but I’d rather not just keep doing this. And of course in Tony’s case he went from being very, very, very busy to being not-so-busy, so the decision got to be easier. In the last year that I was with him it looked like there were twelve weeks of work scheduled for the year and prior to that it was practically the whole year. So I said well —
What year was that, do you recall?
